plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a uniform thin disk twice, in two side-by-side views. The left view looks straight down the rotation axis: a blue-shaded circle with x pointing up, y pointing right, and z labeled at the center where the axis emerges from the page. A double-headed arrow from center to outer edge is labeled R, a second arrow labeled r reaches a thin orange ring concentric with the rim, and a short arrow labeled dr points at that ring's width. The right view redraws the disk in oblique perspective as a shaded ellipse with an orange rim, z vertical, y to the right, x coming toward the lower left; a curved arrow loops around z to show the sense of rotation, and an arrow labeled r runs from the center to an element on the ring labeled dm. Showing the ring face-on and in perspective ties the annular strip of width dr to the mass element dm at one distance from the axis. The pairing motivates finding the moment of inertia by summing thin rings, each carrying all its mass at radius r.

interactionPlan.concept: A uniform disk's moment of inertia is built by summing thin concentric rings, each carrying all its mass at one radius r, so dI = r² dm and the r² factor makes outer mass dominate the total.
elements: Left panel: x-axis (up) and y-axis (right) crossing at center, z labeled at the center where the rotation axis emerges from the page
Left panel: blue-gray shaded circular disk of outer radius R (face-on view)
Left panel: double-headed arrow from center to rim labeled R
Left panel: arrow from center to the highlighted ring labeled r
Left panel: orange concentric annular ring (the differential element) at radius r with width dr
Left panel: short double-headed arrow across the ring width labeled dr
Right panel: oblique shaded elliptical disk with orange rim (perspective view of the same disk)
Right panel: vertical z-axis, horizontal y-axis (right), and x-axis toward the lower-left
Right panel: curved arrow looping around the z-axis indicating sense of rotation
Right panel: arrow from center to a point on the ring labeled r, with that mass element labeled dm
Contribution indicator (bar or numeric readout) proportional to r²·dm that grows as the ring moves outward

interactions.label: Ring radius r
interactions.teaches: Dragging the orange annulus from the center toward the rim moves the matching dm marker in both views and makes the r²·dm contribution grow quadratically, showing why mass farther from the axis contributes disproportionately more to the moment of inertia

interactions.label: Ring width dr
interactions.teaches: Widening or narrowing the highlighted ring changes the shaded strip area and the amount of mass dm it carries, making clear that a thin differential ring is the element being summed over r

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching emphasis between the circular face-on disk and the tilted perspective disk shows the same highlighted annulus in both, confirming the integration element is a complete ring at one radius wrapping all the way around the rotation axis

demo_steps.title: The ring as the element
demo_steps.narration: The disk is split into thin concentric rings; in the face-on view the orange annulus has radius r and width dr, and in the perspective view the same ring carries a mass element dm at distance r from the z-axis.

demo_steps.title: Sweep r outward
demo_steps.narration: Drag the radius slider from the center to the rim: the annulus and the dm marker travel outward together while the r²·dm indicator climbs steeply, revealing the quadratic weighting of outer mass.

demo_steps.title: Shrink the ring to a differential
demo_steps.narration: Narrow dr and watch the shaded strip and its dm shrink toward a true differential element — the thing you integrate from r = 0 to r = R to obtain I = ½MR².

demo_steps.title: See the full ring in perspective
demo_steps.narration: Focus the perspective view: the curved arrow around z and the highlighted rim show that every point of the annulus sits at the same radius r, which is exactly why a ring (not a patch) is the correct element.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because every point of a thin concentric ring lies at the same distance r from the axis, the ring's whole mass contributes r² dm at once — and that r² factor is why the disk's outer mass dominates its moment of inertia.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on a white background. Left: a soft blue-gray filled circle with thin gray x (up) and y (right) axes crossing at center, a small 'z' at the center, a black double-headed arrow to the rim labeled R, an arrow to the ring labeled r, a bright orange concentric annulus, and a short double-headed arrow across its width labeled dr. Right: the same disk drawn as a shaded oblique ellipse with an orange rim, vertical z-axis with a curved rotation arrow looping around it, y-axis to the right, x-axis to the lower-left, and an arrow from center to a rim point labeled r with that element labeled dm. Keep the orange annulus color identical in both panels so the toggle reads as the same ring seen two ways. Add a small horizontal bar or numeric readout near the panels proportional to r²·dr that visibly lengthens as r increases; this is the visual payoff for the radius slider. Use serif italic math styling for R, r, dr, dm, x, y, z labels.

authoredContext:
Integrating to find the moment of inertia of a two-dimensional object is a little bit trickier, but one shape is commonly done at this level of study—a uniform thin disk about an axis through its center (the figure).

Calculating the moment of inertia for a thin disk about an axis through its center.

Figure shows a uniform thin disk of radius r that rotates about a Z axis that passes through its center.

Since the disk is thin, we can take the mass as distributed entirely in the xy-plane. We again start with the relationship for the surface mass density, which is the mass per unit surface area. Since it is uniform, the surface mass density σ is constant:

action_items: Fix the element-reference bug: in SVG.js, group.add(child) returns the GROUP, not the child, so 'leftRArr = gLeft.add(sArrow(...))' stores the group and 'leftRArr.plot(...)' throws. Create the element first, then add it: e.g. 'var leftRArr = sArrow(0,0,0,0); gLeft.add(leftRArr);' and likewise for leftRlbl, leftDrArr, leftDrlbl, rightRArr, rightRlbl, rightDmlbl.
After fixing references, verify redraw() runs without exception so both panels, the orange annulus, the R/r/dr/dm arrows, axis labels, and the contribution bar actually appear.
Confirm the demo-step player and the r / dr sliders visibly move the annulus and dm marker once the crash is resolved.
